zhejiang-museum-history.name: The History of the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Founded in November 1929, the Zhejiang Museum is one of the earliest regional comprehensive museums in China. It was once known as the 'Zhejiang West Lake Museum' and the 'Provincial West Lake Museum'. Its beginnings lie right by West Lake, closely tied to the legacy of the modern West Lake Exposition.

After the West Lake Exposition closed in November 1929, the Zhejiang provincial government set up the Zhejiang West Lake Museum at the southern foot of Solitary Hill (Gushan), using the Wenglan Pavilion, the Wang Yangming Shrine, the Shengyin Arhat Hall and the Taiyi Fenqing Studio to preserve the exposition's relics, with Chen Qihuai appointed director. In February 1930 it was renamed the 'Provincial West Lake Museum'. In May 1949 it was taken over by the People's Liberation Army entering Hangzhou. On 29 September 1993 the new building was completed, covering 2.04 hectares with a total floor area of 7,360 square metres, built at a cost of 20 million yuan.

Since then it has remained at the forefront of Chinese museums: on 1 January 2004 it became the first provincial museum in the country to open free of charge year-round; in 2008 it was rated among the first batch of 'National First-Class Museums'; and in 2009 it was designated a 'Nationally and Locally Co-Built National Museum' by the State Administration of Cultural Heritage and the Ministry of Finance. In December that year, the Wulin campus was completed and opened.

Keep this history in mind as you explore: the milestones from 1929 to 2004 - Chen Qihuai, the Solitary Hill buildings and free admission - together trace a thread running through a century of cultural life around West Lake.

gushan-campus.name: The Gushan Campus and 'A Museum in a Garden, a Garden in a Museum'

blocks.text: The Gushan Campus is the oldest campus of the Zhejiang Museum, set at the southern foot of Solitary Hill (Gushan) by West Lake in Hangzhou. It adjoins the Bai Causeway and the 'Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake' scenic spot to the east and the Xiling Seal Art Society to the west. Completed in the autumn of 1993 and covering 20,400 square metres, its buildings form a layout described as 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum'.

The campus also includes the Zhejiang West Lake Art Museum and the Wenglan Pavilion. The Wenglan Pavilion stands on the west side of the campus. Built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong reign), it was one of the seven imperial pavilions holding copies of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku Quanshu) in the Qing dynasty. Destroyed by fire in 1861 (the 11th year of the Xianfeng reign) and rebuilt in 1880 (the 6th year of the Guangxu reign), it is the only survivor of the three southern pavilions. In 2001 the State Council designated it a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; in 2006 it underwent the largest restoration since the founding of the People's Republic, and it reopened to the public in June 2013.

The main building, completed on 29 September 1993, and the pre-existing gardens of Gushan together make up this 'museum within a garden'. Use the phrase 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum' as your route: first take in the ceramics and calligraphy and paintings in the main hall, then walk to the Wenglan Pavilion and feel how the museum's boundary almost dissolves into the landscape of West Lake.

Most new exhibitions have now moved to the Zhijiang Campus, but Gushan remains the spiritual home of the museum. If you want to understand how a museum can live in harmony with a lake and its hills, the Gushan Campus is the most direct answer.

zhijiang-campus.name: The Zhijiang Campus and 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang'

blocks.text: The Zhijiang Campus is the new main venue of the Zhejiang Museum. Located in the Zhijiang Cultural Center of Hangzhou, it opened to the public on 29 August 2023, covering about 54,400 square metres with a floor area of 100,000 square metres.

Its core is the permanent exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture', spread over the first and second floors and divided into three galleries: 'From Prehistory to the Sui and Tang Dynasties', 'Wuyue and the Two Song Dynasties', and 'From the Yuan, Ming and Qing Dynasties to the Modern Era'. It traces Zhejiang's history from the Paleolithic to 1921 and opened in August 2023. All five groups of artefacts on the national list prohibited from exhibition abroad are on display in this exhibition.

The third floor also houses the permanent exhibition 'Eastward Lies the Ocean - Zhejiang's Maritime Culture', covering about 1,000 square metres. The galleries below the third floor are arranged in chronological order, offering a complementary thread alongside 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang'.

For most visitors, the Zhijiang Campus is the smoothest entry point to the whole of Zhejiang's history: follow the three galleries from prehistory to the modern era, then turn back to examine the museum's treasures and the artefacts barred from overseas exhibition - and the thread of ten thousand years becomes clear.

museum-collection-system.name: A Collection of Over One Hundred Thousand Objects and Its System

blocks.text: The Zhejiang Museum holds more than one hundred thousand artefacts that span virtually every period of Zhejiang's history, a comprehensive regional collection built up through local archaeology and donations.

Highlights of the collection include Hemudu culture pottery, lacquerware, woodwork and ivory artefacts; Liangzhu culture jades and silk; the swords of the Yue kings; celadon from the Yue kiln, the Longquan kiln and the Southern Song Guan (imperial) kiln; mirrors from Kuaiji and Huzhou; works by renowned painters and calligraphers such as Wu Changshuo, Huang Binhong and Sha Menghai; and the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains by the Yuan-dynasty painter Huang Gongwang.

The collection has also grown through donations: on 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated artefacts including 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals; in December 1957, Wu Changshuo's family donated artefacts; in May 1991 the 'Ma Dingxiang Chinese Numismatics Research Center' was established; and in January 2012, Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong donated 160 pieces of lacquerware from the Song to the Qing dynasties.

Faced with more than one hundred thousand objects, you need not see every one. The most efficient way to visit is to follow the two threads of the 'top treasures of the museum' and the 'artefacts barred from overseas exhibition', then choose one category that matches your interest and look deeper.

top-ten-treasures.name: The Selection of the Top Ten Treasures

blocks.text: In June 2009, to mark the 80th anniversary of its founding, the Zhejiang Museum launched a 'Top Ten Treasures' selection. Over the course of one month, a combination of visitor votes and expert opinion produced a list of the ten most representative artefacts in the collection.

The ten treasures chosen were: the Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue (Warring States period); the Ten-Thousand-Work Sedan Chair (Republic of China era); the gilded silver Asoka Pagoda of Wuyue (Five Dynasties period); the Liangzhu culture jade cong; the Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' (The Phoenix Sings in Color); Huang Gongwang's 'Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (Remaining Mountain Scroll)' (Yuan dynasty); the Spring and Autumn bronze house of musicians; the Hemudu culture ivory carving of twin birds facing the sun; the Yuan Longquan kiln boat-shaped water dropper; and the painted clay standing bodhisattva of the Northern Song dynasty.

Spanning from the Neolithic Hemudu and Liangzhu cultures to the Republican era, these ten objects are a microcosm of the museum's collection system: jade, porcelain, lacquer, painting and calligraphy, bronze, ivory carving and clay sculpture - categories of every kind.
Treat this list as a self-guided route: hunt them down one by one through the galleries, and with each one you find, you understand a little more of Zhejiang's craft and history.

Some of China's most important artefacts are placed by the state on a national list barring them from overseas exhibition. They may only be shown within China and may not be lent abroad for touring shows. Five groups of artefacts at the Zhejiang Museum are on this list.

On 18 January 2002, the State Administration of Cultural Heritage issued the First Catalogue of Artefacts Barred from Overseas Exhibition, listing 64 objects, of which three were held by the Zhejiang Museum, including the King Jade Cong unearthed at Liangzhu, kept by the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology. In the Third Catalogue, announced on 19 August 2013, two more artefacts from the Zhejiang Museum were included.

All five groups of artefacts are displayed in the exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' at the Zhijiang Campus. In other words, walk the full length of this exhibition and you will see all five national treasures barred from overseas exhibition in one go.
Take 'barred from overseas exhibition' as an important hint as you look around: anything on this list is a core artefact deserving special protection and especially careful viewing.

The Hemudu culture was a Neolithic culture distributed across the plains on the southern shore of Hangzhou Bay in Zhejiang, China, extending to the Zhoushan Islands, dating from roughly 6,000 to 7,000 years ago. It takes its name from the Hemudu site in Yuyao, where it was first excavated.

The site has yielded extensive remains of stilt houses (ganlan buildings) and cultivated rice, along with plant remains such as gourds, acorns, water chestnuts and jujubes, and domestic animals including pigs, dogs and water buffalo. Stone tools are relatively few; wood and bone implements predominate. Among the finds are China's earliest wooden ornament, a carved wooden fish, and the earliest lacquerware yet discovered in China.

The Hemudu culture was first identified in 1973, and the Hemudu site was excavated in two campaigns in 1973-1974 and 1977-1978. In the 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang' exhibition at the Zhijiang Campus, Hemudu pottery, bone ploughs and lacquered woodwork are often among the first artefacts visitors encounter.

As you face the Hemudu exhibits, ponder this: stilt houses, cultivated rice and domesticated animals all appear together, showing that the people here already knew how to run their own lives in the watery landscape of Hangzhou Bay six or seven thousand years ago.

hemudu-double-bird.name: Ivory Carving of Twin Birds Facing the Sun

blocks.text: The ivory carving of twin birds facing the sun is a masterpiece of line engraving from the Hemudu culture and one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It was made by the Hemudu people of the Neolithic age, some 6,000 to 7,000 years ago.

The carving is 16.6 cm long, 5.9 cm across at its widest surviving point and 1.2 cm thick. At its centre, five concentric circles form a sun motif, encircled by a ring of flame patterns, while on either side two birds with hooked beaks look up and face each other. It is the finest example of the line-engraving craft of the Hemudu site.
Among the same group of Hemudu ivory objects there are works best known for the 'double fire bird' motif, showing that birds and the sun were themes the Hemudu people returned to again and again.

When you come upon this carving in the gallery, first look at the concentric-circle sun at its centre, then the two birds gazing up at each other on either side - an imagining of light and birds from seven thousand years ago, preserved to this day through a few engraved lines.

Dating from 5,300 to 4,000 years ago, the Liangzhu culture was a Neolithic archaeological culture of China that arose and developed in the region around Lake Taihu in the lower Yangtze. More than 500 sites have been discovered, with Mojiaoshan, near the Liangzhu site, at their centre.

The most distinctive feature of the Liangzhu culture is the use and burial of jades, including large cong tubes, bi discs and yue axes. The cong is the most finely crafted and most authoritative of these jades, often engraved with delicate beast-face patterns that were regarded as images of deities, while the yue axe symbolized military and royal power. The Liangzhu people also farmed skillfully with stone ploughs, rice became the principal food source, and a proto-writing system appeared.

The Liangzhu political organization was a chiefdom, though some scholars argue it already resembled an incipient state. It could mobilize large numbers of laborers to build grand ritual precincts, city walls and flood-control embankments, and its society was stratified into aristocratic and commoner classes. The beast-face motifs on Liangzhu jades share many features with the taotie motifs on Shang dynasty bronzes; the scholar Li Xueqin held that, while not a direct inheritance, the connection was close.

When viewing Liangzhu artefacts, fix your eye on the forms and beast-face patterns of the cong, bi and yue, and you can read from jade object after jade object a prehistoric society skilled at organizing labor and devoted to the ritual of jade.

liangzhu-cong-wang.name: The King Jade Cong of Liangzhu

blocks.text: The King Jade Cong of Liangzhu comes from Tomb 12 at Fanshan. Weighing 3,500 grams and engraved with exquisite beast-face patterns, it is regarded by scholars as the 'king of cong tubes' and is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum.

Tomb 12 at Fanshan is one of the highest-ranking burials in the Liangzhu aristocratic cemetery. Besides the King Cong, it also yielded a superbly made jade yue axe regarded as the 'king of yue axes', with a wooden handle 70-80 cm long fitted with jade fittings at both ends - a symbol of military and royal power. Tomb 20 at Fanshan, containing as many as 547 jade objects, is thought to be the burial of the supreme leader.

The cong was a ritual object used in sacrifices to the earth. The ancients believed that 'the heavens are round and the earth is square', so they offered round bi discs to heaven and square cong tubes to earth. The jade of Liangzhu came from a tremolite deposit at Xiaomeiling, in the foothills of the Tianmu Mountains at Liyang, Jiangsu. Today this King Jade Cong is on the list of artefacts barred from overseas exhibition and is displayed in the 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang' gallery at the Zhijiang Campus.

When you view the King Cong, first take in its square exterior, round inner bore and four projecting corners, then study the beast-face patterns engraved on each side. You will see it is at once the summit of Liangzhu craftsmanship and a ritual object linking heaven and earth.

liangzhu-heritage.name: The Liangzhu Ancient City Site and World Heritage

blocks.text: The Liangzhu site lies in Liangzhu Subdistrict and Pingyao Town of Yuhang District, Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China, with part extending into Xiazhu Lake Subdistrict of Deqing County, Huzhou. It is a cluster of sites centred on the Liangzhu Ancient City site, covering 34 square kilometres in total and dating from 3300 to 2000 BC.

The Liangzhu Ancient City site is the most important and representative site of the Liangzhu culture, hailed as 'China's first city' and 'living proof of five thousand years of Chinese civilization'. On 6 July 2019, meeting criteria (iii) and (iv), it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

The city site comprises a palace area, an inner city and an outer city, covering 881.45 hectares. The surrounding water management system included high dams at mountain valleys, low dams on the plain and a long levee at the foot of the hills, the last known as the Tangshan site, about five kilometres in total length. The Liangzhu site was placed on China's Tentative List for World Heritage in 1994, designated a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level (4th batch) in 1996, and named among the first National Archaeological Site Parks by the State Administration of Cultural Heritage on 9 October 2010.

Many of the cong and bi jades you see in the museum come from this World Heritage site cluster. Connect these jades with the name 'Liangzhu Ancient City' as you look, and each artefact will carry you back to that waterbound city-state bearing witness to five thousand years of civilization.

cong-ritual-jade.name: The Cong: A Ritual Object for Sacrificing to the Earth

blocks.text: The cong is an ancient Chinese tubular jade object used in sacrifices: square on the outside with a round bore. Its earliest appearances are found in the third phase of the Xuejiagang culture at Qianshan, Anhui, some 5,100 years ago.

Among jades, the cong was the object used to sacrifice to the earth. The ancients believed that 'the heavens are round and the earth is square', so they offered round bi discs to heaven and square cong tubes to earth. The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) records: 'Six objects were made of jade to honor heaven, earth and the four directions: a dark-green bi to honor heaven, and a yellow cong to honor earth.'

Curiously, when a jade cong was unearthed during the reign of the Qianlong emperor, nobody knew what it was for. Qianlong himself concluded it was a counterweight used by the ancients to move heavy objects; he named it 'gangtou' (pole end) and fitted it with a copper lining to use as a brush pot or vase. Only more than 90 years after his death was it identified as the ritual object we now call the cong.

Look again at the Liangzhu cong in the gallery, and first remember 'square outside, round within': the square is the earth, the circle the heavens - a single cong holds in your hand the ancient imagination of cosmic order.

yue-bronze-swords.name: The Bronze Sword Tradition of the Yue State

blocks.text: The state of Yue was one of the principal sources of smelting materials such as copper and tin in the pre-Qin period. That the Yue people excelled at making swords and blades was a universally acknowledged fact before the Western Han. Works such as the Rites of Zhou, the Zhuangzi, the Strategies of the Warring States and the Huainanzi all praise the quality of Yue weapons. Yue also boasted the renowned swordmaker Ou Yezi and the sword connoisseur Xue Zhu.

The 'Artificers' Record' of the Rites of Zhou notes that 'the swords of Wu and Yue... cannot be made as fine anywhere else', and the Zhuangzi likewise says, 'The swords of Gan and Yue are kept in their scabbards and not dared to be used - they are treasured above all.' So precious were the swords of Wu and Yue in their day. The Sword of King Goujian of Yue unearthed today has been shown to use a copper-sulfide anti-corrosion technique - the Yue people had already mastered composite-metal craftsmanship.

Unlike the central plain states, which emphasized chariot warfare, the southern states of Wu and Yue fought mostly in close-order infantry battles, and infantry made up the core of the Yue army. Bronze objects of Yue unearthed in modern times - the Sword of King Goujian and the Sword of King Zhejiyushi - bear this tradition out.

As you stand before the Yue sword case, look closely at the inscriptions and the colour of the bronze on the blades - behind a sword 'treasured above all' lies the whole bronze-casting tradition of Wu and Yue.

zhejiang-yue-sword.name: The Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue

blocks.text: The Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue is a bronze sword cast during the reign of King Zhejiyushi of the Spring and Autumn period. It is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. Although Zhejiyushi reigned for only six years, he had bronze swords cast in great numbers.

King Zhejiyushi of Yue is the Shiyu recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian as the son of King Goujian. His name appears as 'Yuyi' in the Yue Jue Shu and as 'Luying' in the Bamboo Annals. According to the Bamboo Annals, Luying reigned for six years, from 464 to 459 BC in the Western calendar.

Swords of this kind reflect many facets of the bronze smelting and casting technology of the Wu-Yue region. Inscribed Yue king swords are relatively rare finds and are usually works of superb craftsmanship. Known examples bear the names of the kings Goujian, Zhejiyushi, Bushou, Zhougou, Buguang and Jibeigu.

When you view this sword, first read the inscription on the blade or the guard, then reflect on its owner's story - a son of Goujian who reigned six years yet cast swords in profusion for posterity. A single weapon thus links the Records of the Grand Historian with an object before your eyes.

wuyue-state.name: The Wuyue Kingdom and Its Policy of Protecting the Realm

blocks.text: Wuyue (16 June 907 - 9 June 978) was one of the Ten Kingdoms of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Founded by Qian Liu in 907 with its capital at Hangzhou (the 'Western Capital'), it was the only state never conquered by force during the Northern Song's founding wars.

At the height of its power Wuyue ruled thirteen prefectures, roughly corresponding to the whole of today's Zhejiang province, southeastern Jiangsu and northeastern Fujian. From 902, when Emperor Zhaozong of Tang enfeoffed Qian Liu as King of Yue, to 978, when Qian Chu surrendered to the Northern Song, Wuyue passed through five kings over 72 years. On 9 June 978, Qian Hongchu offered his territory to the Song, bringing the Wuyue regime to an end.

Pressed by the landward military threats of the neighbouring Wu kingdom and the Southern Tang, Wuyue vigorously developed maritime trade. The Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties records that boats crowded the capital Hangzhou 'so densely that neither bow nor stern could be seen'; the Northern Song writer Su Shi called its wealth in ivory, rhinoceros horn, pearls and jade 'the finest under heaven'. Under a policy of protecting the realm and reassuring the people, the economy prospered, and the profits of fishing, salt, sericulture and mulberry farming surpassed all of Jiangnan.

In the Wuyue and Song gallery of 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang', picture Leifeng Pagoda, Baochu Pagoda and the surrounding West Lake relics as the skyline of the Wuyue kingdom - a realm that prospered through seafaring and stability, and the very image of Zhejiang in the Five Dynasties.

wuyue-buddhist-art.name: Wuyue Buddhism and the Jewel Casket Stupa

blocks.text: Buddhism was a central part of Wuyue culture, and every king of Wuyue was a devout believer. By the reign of King Zhongyi the kingdom boasted 84,000 stupas and pagodas, including such famous ones as Hangzhou's Baochu Pagoda and Leifeng Pagoda today.

The jewel casket stupa - also called the 'baogieyin ta', the gold-painted tower or the Asoka pagoda - is a type of solid tower, square in plan, made up of four parts: a base, a body, an eave and a spire. The eaves turn up at the four corners of the body in what is called the 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' (shanhua jiaoye) form. The type developed from the ancient Indian stupa and entered China via Nepal.

In the Five Dynasties period, King Qian Hongchu of Wuyue, imitating King Asoka, had 84,000 pagodas built, spreading the jewel casket stupa widely and leaving behind many remains. Under Wuyue's Buddhist atmosphere, block printing in Hangzhou flourished; in the reign of King Zhongyi (Qian Chu) alone, as many as 662,000 scrolls of sutras and images of Buddhas were printed.

When you see a jewel casket stupa such as the gilded silver Asoka Pagoda in the gallery, first look at the four 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' corners of the crown, then think of the Wuyue king who 'built 84,000 pagodas' - a small stupa holds the shadow of an entire Buddhist kingdom.

asoka-pagoda.name: The Five Dynasties Gilded Silver Asoka Pagoda

blocks.text: The Five Dynasties Wuyue gilded silver Asoka Pagoda is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. A small pagoda-shaped artefact of the jewel casket stupa type, it came from the excavation of the Leifeng Pagoda site.

The underground palace of Leifeng Pagoda, opened on 11 March 2001, was a brick-built vertical shaft. At its centre stood an iron reliquary casket, surrounded by offerings symbolizing the 'Seven Treasures' and other Buddhist artefacts. Altogether 51 groups of objects were unearthed from the underground palace, the most important being a gilded pure-silver Asoka Pagoda. Inside its body was a golden container wrapped with thin gold leaf into the shape of a coffin, presumably enshrining a relic of the Buddha's spiral hair. Together with the pure-silver Asoka Pagoda, it ranks among the most important objects from the site.

Both Asoka pagodas are square in form, composed of a base, a body, four banana-leaf-like 'mountain flowers' and a spire, with scenes from the Buddha's jataka (past-life) stories engraved on all four sides of the body. Most of the many artefacts unearthed at Leifeng Pagoda in 2000-2001 are now collected and displayed at the Zhejiang Museum.

As you look at this gilded little pagoda, first take in the banana-leaf corners and the engraved scenes on its body, then recall that it rested at the very centre of the Leifeng Pagoda underground palace for a thousand years - the most direct physical evidence of the Wuyue Buddhist kingdom and of the pagoda history of Hangzhou.

yue-kiln.name: The Yue Kiln and Secret-Colour Celadon

blocks.text: The Yue kiln was a porcelain kiln of Shaoxing's Yue Prefecture in Zhejiang during the Tang and Five Dynasties periods, with its main kiln sites spread around Shanglin Lake in Cixi. As Shaoxing was called 'Yue Prefecture' under the Sui and Tang dynasties, the kiln took the name 'Yue'.

In his Classic of Tea, the Tang writer Lu Yu wrote: 'For bowls, Yue Prefecture is the finest. Its porcelain resembles jade and ice.' In the late Tang and Five Dynasties, the finest Yue kiln celadon, with its green of 'a thousand peaks', was reserved exclusively as tribute for the court; commoners were not permitted to use it, which is why it was called 'secret colour' (mise).

On 3 April 1987, the underground palace of the Famen Temple pagoda was opened, yielding thirteen pieces of secret-colour porcelain, now kept at the Famen Temple Museum. In the late Northern Song, as ceramic techniques coarsened, the Yue kiln declined; in the mid Southern Song, it ceased production altogether.

As you look at Yue celadon, weigh the phrase 'like jade, like ice' against the body of a piece, then consider the kiln's rise and fall from the golden age of the Tang to the Song - the very source of Chinese celadon laid out before you in the cases.

longquan-kiln.name: The Longquan Kiln and Its Powder-Blue and Plum-Green Glazes

blocks.text: Longquan celadon was a system of kilns centred on the ancient kiln sites of Longquan city in Zhejiang, with branches spread widely across the surrounding region. The Longquan kiln is generally held to have reached its golden age in the Southern Song.

By improving glaze recipes, the Longquan kiln created unprecedented shades such as powder blue (fencing) and plum green (meizi qing), admired by collectors through the ages and earning the kiln a place among the famous kilns of the Song dynasty. Glazes fell into two types, lime glazes and lime-alkali glazes. The Northern Song used lime glazes; the Southern Song used lime-alkali glazes, which could be applied in multiple coats to build up a thick glaze layer - the powder-blue glaze is of this lime-alkali type.

Firing temperatures at the Longquan kiln ranged from 1,180 to 1,230 C; plum green required the highest heat, 1,250 to 1,280 C. In September 2009, the traditional firing techniques of Longquan celadon were inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Compare the powder-blue and plum-green glazes side by side, and gesture how thick the glaze feels, and you will understand how Southern Song craftsmen used lime-alkali glaze to render green as warm and smooth as jade.

longquan-boat-drip.name: The Yuan Longquan Kiln Boat-Shaped Water Dropper

blocks.text: The Yuan Longquan kiln boat-shaped water dropper is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It is a celadon scholar's object of the Longquan kiln family - a small vessel used in the study to hold water for grinding ink.

The Longquan kiln flourished in the Southern Song, when improved glaze recipes produced shades such as powder blue and plum green. Fashioned in the shape of a little boat, this water dropper is a fine example of the scholar's objects of Longquan celadon - practical, and full of the elegant charm of the literati study.

After passing the large Longquan dishes and bowls in the ceramics gallery, encountering this little boat that fits in the palm makes you appreciate that the Longquan kiln produced not only grand wares but also something so delicate and light.

As you look at it, reflect: though the water dropper is tiny, it must both store water and release it drop by drop - a piece of celadon that fuses the beauty of an object with the daily act of writing.

The Southern Song Guan Kiln Campus of the Hangzhou West Lake Museum (formerly the Southern Song Guan Kiln Museum) is located in Hangzhou, Zhejiang. Built on the site of the Southern Song imperial kiln at Jiaotanxia, it is the first museum in China devoted to ceramics and built around an ancient kiln site, and the most direct place to learn about the Southern Song Guan kiln.

The Southern Song Guan Kiln Museum covers about 43,000 square metres with 10,000 square metres of exhibition space. It opened to the public in 1992, underwent comprehensive renovation in 2002, a second-phase expansion in 2007, and completed a third-phase expansion in 2010. In April 2020 it was merged with the Hangzhou West Lake Museum and the Hangzhou Museum of Famous People into the Hangzhou West Lake Museum headquarters.

Founded on the Jiaotanxia kiln site in Hangzhou, the Southern Song Guan kiln, together with the Yue and Longquan kilns, forms a key link in the genealogy of Zhejiang celadon. Southern Song Guan celadon is also an important part of the ceramic collection of the Zhejiang Museum.

If, after visiting the Zhejiang Museum, you still want to go deeper into the history of ceramics, make a special trip to the Southern Song Guan Kiln Campus at the Jiaotanxia site, where kiln site and galleries stand together - there you can go from firing temperatures and glazes all the way to the remains of the kilns themselves.

fuchun-shanju-tu.name: The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains and the Remaining Mountain Scroll

blocks.text: The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains is the work of Huang Gongwang, a painter active at the end of the Song and the beginning of the Yuan dynasty. Painted between 1347 and 1350 against the backdrop of the Fuchun River in Zhejiang, it is his masterpiece, praised by later generations as the 'Lanting of painting' and the 'supreme divine work of landscape painting', and it is counted among China's ten greatest surviving paintings.

In the early Qing, under the Shunzhi emperor, the painting passed to Wu Hongyu. Before his death, Wu decided to have the painting buried with him, and when it was thrown into the fire, his nephew Wu Zhendu rescued it from the flames - but the scroll had been burned into two sections, one large and one small. The small opening section, repaired, is known as the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll', measuring 51.4 cm wide and 31.8 cm high, about one-fourteenth of the original; the longer section is the 'Scroll for Master Wuyong', 636.9 cm wide and 33 cm high, about twelve-fourteenths of the original.

The Zhejiang Museum treasures precisely this 'Remaining Mountain Scroll'; it, too, was chosen among the museum's top ten treasures. On 2 June 2011, the Remaining Mountain Scroll and the National Palace Museum's Scroll for Master Wuyong were shown together at the Taipei palace museum, the two originals displayed side by side in a single case sixteen metres long.

As you view the Remaining Mountain Scroll, first think of its story: a fire split the long scroll in two, one part staying in Hangzhou and one going to Taiwan - and this small section before you is where that story begins.

huang-gongwang.name: Huang Gongwang and the Fuchun River

blocks.text: Huang Gongwang (1269-1354), courtesy name Zijiu, with the sobriquets Dachi, Dachi Daoren and Yifeng Daoren, was a Yuan-dynasty painter from Changshu Prefecture, Pingjiang Circuit (today's Changshu, Suzhou, Jiangsu). Honoured as the first of the 'Four Great Masters of the Yuan', he is named alongside Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng.

Huang Gongwang did not begin studying painting until he was fifty. Guided by Zhao Mengfu, he originated the 'light crimson' (qianjiang) landscape style, and his ink landscapes were particularly accomplished. His masterpiece is the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, and his treatise Notes on Landscape Painting is an important theoretical work of Chinese landscape painting.

In September 1315 (the 2nd year of Yanyou), Huang Gongwang was imprisoned after being implicated in the corruption case of Zhang Lu. After his release he entered the Quanzhen Daoist order. On the 25th day of the 10th month of 1354 (the 14th year of Zhizheng), he died in Changshu and was buried at the western foot of Mount Yu.

After seeing the Remaining Mountain Scroll at the Zhejiang Museum, spare a thought for the painter who took up art at fifty yet turned the Fuchun River into the 'Lanting of painting': his humble start and late flowering are themselves a story worth reading slowly.

huang-binhong.name: Huang Binhong and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Huang Binhong (27 January 1865 - 25 March 1955), personal name Zhi, courtesy names Pucun and Puren, and known by the sobriquets Yuxiang, Honglu and Hongsou, adopted the name Binhong in middle age and is known by it. Born in Jinhua, Zhejiang, with ancestral roots in Tandu village, western She County, Anhui, he was a modern Chinese landscape painter.

On 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated his collections: 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals. According to another account, after Huang's death his family, honouring his last wish, donated all the more than five thousand of his works and over ten thousand artefacts, manuscripts and other belongings to the Zhejiang Museum.

In March 1958, the Zhejiang Museum established the Huang Binhong Memorial Room at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, Hangzhou. In the summer of 1948, the 85-year-old Huang, invited by the National Hangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, came south from Beiping and spent the last seven years of his life here. The memorial room formally opened to visitors in 1988.

When you see Huang Binhong's many works and manuscripts in the museum's painting and calligraphy galleries, reflect: this painter, who in his later years pursued a style of 'depth, richness, splendour and vitality', left his life's work to Zhejiang and became one of the great pillars of the museum's collection.

sha-menghai.name: Sha Menghai and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Sha Menghai (11 June 1900 - 10 October 1992), originally named Sha Wenruo, courtesy name Menghai, with the sobriquets Shacun, Lansha, Shihuang and Jueming, came from Sha village in Tangxi township, Yin County, Zhejiang (today's Yinzhou District, Ningbo). He was a Chinese calligrapher and seal carver, and a master whose ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep.

In August 1953, Sha Menghai concurrently served as head of the history department of the Zhejiang Museum. One account has him becoming honorary director of the museum in August 1984; another source says he became honorary director in 1981, the same year he was elected vice-chairman of the Chinese Calligraphers Association. He also became a professor of calligraphy and seal carving at the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1963, was elected director of the Xiling Seal Art Society in 1979, served as head of the Xiling Academy of Calligraphy and Painting in 1980, and was made a lifetime professor of the academy in 1989.

The former residence of Sha Menghai stands at No. 15 Longyou Road, Hangzhou, covering 870 square metres with a total floor area of 601 square metres, a two-storey villa of brick-and-timber construction. The five-character plaque reading 'Former Residence of Sha Menghai' in the courtyard was written by the seal carver and calligrapher Qian Juntao. It formally opened in November 2004.

When you visit the Zhejiang Museum and see its collection of calligraphy and seals, of which Sha Menghai is a representative figure, spare a thought for his ties to the Xiling Seal Art Society and to Gushan - calligraphy, seal carving and the cultural institutions of Zhejiang are joined together in him.

wu-changshuo.name: Wu Changshuo and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Wu Changshuo (12 September 1844 - 29 November 1927) came from Zhangwu village, Anji County, Huzhou, Zhejiang. A seal carver active in the late Qing and early Republic, he was also accomplished in calligraphy and painting.

In 1904, Wu Changshuo became director of the Xiling Seal Art Society on Gushan, Hangzhou, calling himself the 'seal-craving beggar of the five lakes'. He once said he began learning to write poetry at thirty and did not take up painting until fifty. In his later years he settled in Shanghai and was later grouped with the 'Shanghai School' (Haipai). His works include the Collected Poems of Foulu, the Collected Seals of Foulu and the Album of Paintings by Wu Changshuo.
In December 1957, Wu Changshuo's family donated artefacts to the Zhejiang Museum, making his works part of the museum's painting and calligraphy collection.

As you look at the museum's paintings, calligraphy and seals, set Wu Changshuo's works beside his remark about 'taking up painting at fifty' - late blooming yet tireless, exactly the shared temperament of the Shanghai School and the painting-and-calligraphy tradition of Zhejiang.

guqin-world.name: The Guqin and the Chinese World of Sound

blocks.text: The guqin (seven-stringed zither) is one of the oldest instruments in Chinese history and an object through which the Chinese have given voice to sound and feeling. On 7 November 2003, the art of the guqin was inscribed by UNESCO on the second Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; on 20 May 2006, the State Council added the guqin to the first national list of intangible cultural heritage.

Guqin making advanced enormously in the Tang dynasty. The 'Jiuxiao Huanpei' and 'Dasheng Yiyin' zithers made for the Tang imperial family by the Lei family of Sichuan are both famous surviving instruments, and Tang zithers have been prized in every age as rare treasures. Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated examples are those made in the Tang, and nearly twenty Tang instruments survive today. As for form, the old saying holds that 'the Tang is round'.

In the Song and Yuan periods distinct schools of guqin began to emerge. The first school, the Zhe school, appeared in the late Southern Song, founded by Guo Mian. Today more than 3,360 guqin pieces, over 130 tablature collections and some 300 guqin songs survive.

Before the guqin cases at the Zhejiang Museum, grow quiet first: study the crackle patterns and inscriptions on the instruments, then consider how an object spanning 'from Tang to Song, from the Lei family to the Zhe school' keeps an aural tradition alive on a wooden body lacquered over.

cai-feng-ming-qi.name: The Tang Seven-Stringed Zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi'

blocks.text: The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' ('A Colorful Phoenix Sings at Qishan') is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. Made in the Tang dynasty, it is a celebrated surviving guqin and a representative piece in the museum's guqin collection.

Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated examples are those of the Tang dynasty; nearly twenty Tang zithers have come down to us and have been treasured in every age as rare treasures. 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' belongs precisely to this group of Tang instruments that have survived to this day.

The art of the guqin was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 7 November 2003 and on the first national intangible cultural heritage list on 20 May 2006. This Tang zither is a tangible example of that ancient art that can still be heard today.

When you see this Tang zither, first look at its name and its face, then reflect that it has been silent for nearly fourteen hundred years - an instrument that has carried the aural tradition of the Tang all the way into today's display case.

qi-lacquer-donation.name: The Lacquerware Donated by Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong

blocks.text: In 2012, the Hong Kong industrialist Mr. Cao Qiyong, a noted native of Zhejiang, and his wife donated 160 pieces (groups) of lacquerware they had treasured for years to the Zhejiang Museum. Spanning from the Song to the Qing dynasties, this collection is an important source of the museum's lacquer holdings.

Appraisal found that the donated lacquerware includes 21 first-grade artefacts, 118 second-grade and 15 third-grade. Among them, the carved red-lacquer (tihong) plate of children at play by the Yuan master carver Zhang Cheng is a national-treasure-grade work, one of only four known pieces bearing the mark 'made by Zhang Cheng'.

In January 2012, Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong donated 160 pieces of lacquerware from the Song to the Qing dynasties to the museum. In the displays at the Zhijiang Campus, this lacquerware, together with bronzes, ceramics and more, reveals another dimension of Zhejiang's craftsmanship.

As you look at this lacquerware, note techniques like tihong (carved red lacquer), where layer after layer of lacquer is applied and then carved, and appreciate how, from Song to Qing, a single lacquer piece took shape through dozens of processes and the accumulation of time.

shili-hongzhuang.name: Shili Hongzhuang and the Marriage Customs of Ningbo and Shaoxing

blocks.text: Shili hongzhuang ('a ten-li red trousseau') is a marriage custom of eastern Zhejiang, centred on Ninghai County. It takes its name from the practice in which a daughter's dowry - from beds and furniture down to needles, thread and headdresses - was so complete that the procession bearing it stretched for ten li (roughly five kilometres). The custom began in the Southern Song and flourished in the Ming and Qing dynasties.

In 2008, the shili hongzhuang wedding custom was inscribed on China's national intangible cultural heritage list. The local Ninghai crafts of vermilion-and-gold woodcarving (zhujin mudiao) and gold-ground painted lacquer (nijin caiqi) provided the technical support for making these exquisite dowries. Ninghai dowries centre on vermilion-and-gold woodcarving and mainly include bridal sedan chairs, wedding beds, carrying cases, vessels and various ornaments, giving rise to the saying of the 'thousand-work bed and ten-thousand-work sedan chair'.

According to legend, in the late Northern Song, the Prince of Kang, Zhao Gou, fleeing pursuit by the Jin army in eastern Zhejiang, was rescued by a country girl. After he took the throne as Emperor Gaozong, he decreed that all women of eastern Zhejiang might be granted royal honours and ride in dragon-and-phoenix bridal sedan chairs on their wedding day. During the Cultural Revolution, shili hongzhuang objects were badly damaged as 'the four olds'. In the early reform era, many Westerners rushed to Ninghai to buy them up, and artefacts were lost on a serious scale; the Ninghai antique dealer He Xiaodao began to collect shili hongzhuang artefacts, and in 2003 the Shili Hongzhuang Museum opened.

When you see the wedding beds, sedan chairs and vessels of shili hongzhuang at the Zhejiang Museum, picture them as a trousseau procession on the move: from Ninghai to Hangzhou, vermilion-and-gold woodcarving and gold-ground painted lacquer carried the joy of marriage and the skill of the craftsmen right into the museum.

The Republican-era ten-thousand-work sedan chair is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It is the most magnificent and massive item of dowry in the shili hongzhuang marriage custom of the Ningbo-Shaoxing region.

Dowries in Ninghai custom centre on vermilion-and-gold woodcarving, giving rise to the saying of the 'thousand-work bed and ten-thousand-work sedan chair'. The bridal sedan was often built of woods such as catalpa, camphor and ginkgo - light yet tough - and covered with carvings of auspicious and festive motifs. It is a representative work of the vermilion-and-gold woodcarving craft.

The term 'ten-thousand-work' is a way of saying that an extraordinary number of man-hours went into it. When you look at this sedan chair, move close to study the dense layers of carved figures and auspicious patterns on its body, then step back to take in the whole silhouette and imagine a crimson trousseau procession stretching for ten li.

shi-xingeng-discovery.name: Shi Xingeng and the Discovery of Liangzhu

blocks.text: The discovery of the Liangzhu culture is closely bound up with Shi Xingeng, a draughtsman at the Zhejiang Museum (then called the West Lake Museum). In December 1936, Shi Xingeng carried out archaeology at Liangzhu township in Yuhang and excavated the site of the 'Liangzhu culture'.

In 1936, Shi Xingeng found a black, glossy potsherd near Qipanfen close to Liangzhu township in Yuhang, and that same year began excavating around the township, uncovering more black pottery and stone tools. In the spring of 1937 he wrote Liangzhu (also titled A Preliminary Report on the Black Pottery Culture Site of the Second District of Hang County), which brought the Liangzhu culture to the attention of the archaeological world.

According to another account, between December 1936 and March 1937 Shi Xingeng carried out three test excavations in the Liangzhu area, identifying twelve sites including Mao'anli and Qipanfen. In 1959, the archaeologist Xia Nai named this cultural type the 'Liangzhu culture'.
As you look at the Liangzhu jades, reflect: these exquisite jades began with a museum draughtsman and a few black potsherds in 1936 - museums and archaeology advance each other in just this way.

jiyue-bronze-house.name: The Spring and Autumn Bronze House of Musicians

blocks.text: The Spring and Autumn bronze house of musicians is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. A bronze object on the theme of a house and its musicians, it comes from the Shaoxing area, the heartland of the state of Yue.

According to historical accounts, the bronze house of musicians unearthed at Shaoxing contains figures of a drummer, zither players, a se player and singing performers, recreating a scene of ensemble singing among the Yue people. It freezes a 'little concert' from more than two thousand years ago in bronze.

The state of Yue was one of the principal sources of smelting materials such as copper and tin in the pre-Qin period, and the skill of the Yue people at making swords and blades was a fact universally acknowledged before the Western Han. The bronze house of musicians is a rare work from this deep bronze-casting tradition that depicts a musical scene.

When you look at this little bronze house, first count the musicians and instruments inside, then think of the bronze world of Yue it belongs to - the people of Zhejiang more than two thousand years ago were already combining drums, qin and se in ensemble performance.

caisu-mud-bodhisattva.name: The Northern Song Painted Clay Standing Bodhisattva

blocks.text: The Northern Song painted clay standing bodhisattva is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum - a polychrome clay sculpture of a bodhisattva from the Song dynasty.

Compared with bronze or porcelain, clay Buddhist images are far harder to preserve; that a painted clay bodhisattva of the Northern Song should survive to this day is remarkable in itself. Like the Buddhist remains of the Five Dynasties Wuyue kingdom, it reminds you, as you look at the sculptures at the Zhejiang Museum, to notice the other path Song sculpture took in materials and form.

hemudu-painted-pottery.name: Decorated Pottery of the Hemudu Culture

blocks.text: The decorated pottery of the Hemudu culture was made by hand by the Hemudu people, with patterns painted or incised on the surface. These pots are important physical evidence for understanding Hemudu life and beliefs. They are thick, grey-black in colour, and often bear cord-marking or motifs of plants and animals.

Hemudu pottery was handmade, very thick, grey-black, often polished on the surface, and commonly decorated with cord marks or carved plant and animal designs. The motifs painted on the pottery include birds, fish, rice, the sun, flowers and grasses, with the fish-and-grain basin, the rice-ear basin, the pig-design bowl and the five-leaf motif pottery plaque as representative pieces.

Hemudu pottery reached a considerable standard; the highest estimated firing temperature was 1,000 C. Another account records that pottery from the first phase of the Hemudu site was fired at about 850 C, mainly by the coiling method. The two excavations yielded 1,695 complete or restored vessels, several times that number in sherds, and carbon-tempered black ware predominates among them.

As you look at these decorated pots, first identify the motifs - birds, fish, rice, the sun, flowers and grasses, the watery everyday life the Hemudu people faced day after day - then consider firing temperatures of nearly a thousand degrees (or, by one account, 850 C) to appreciate what kiln-fire it took to shape such a vessel.

The bone plough is a bone digging tool for turning soil unearthed at the Hemudu site. It was the Hemudu people's trusty implement for tilling the land and planting rice, and it is the emblematic artefact of what is called 'plough-till agriculture'.

The two formal excavations at the Hemudu site yielded about two hundred bone ploughs. Of the 4,670 artefacts recovered in the second formal excavation, bone objects made up 48.6 per cent - a measure of how much bone implements weighed in the Hemudu remains.

Professor You Xiuling of Zhejiang Agricultural University proposed that the bone plough was the tool with which the Hemudu people turned the soil, and he named the farming form of the time 'plough-till agriculture' after it - a view now widely accepted in scholarship. The site also yielded vast quantities of cultivated rice in deposits 40 to 50 cm thick, a sensation in academic circles.

As you look at the bone plough, think of it together with the layer upon layer of cultivated rice: it was with bone tools like this that the Hemudu people turned the soil and planted rice, and thereby took root in the watery landscape of Hangzhou Bay six or seven thousand years ago.

zhang-cheng-red-lacquer.name: Zhang Cheng's Carved Red-Lacquer Plate of Children at Play

blocks.text: Zhang Cheng's carved red-lacquer plate of children at play is a work by the master Yuan lacquer carver Zhang Cheng. It ranks as a national-treasure-grade artefact, one of only four known pieces bearing the mark 'made by Zhang Cheng', and the crowning piece of the Zhejiang Museum's lacquer collection.

The carved red-lacquer plate of children at play by Zhang Cheng, master carver of the Yuan, is a national-treasure-grade work and one of only four known pieces 'made by Zhang Cheng'. In 2012, the noted Zhejiang-born Hong Kong industrialist Mr. Cao Qiyong and his wife donated 160 pieces (groups) of lacquerware they had treasured for years to the Zhejiang Museum - and this plate was among them.

Appraisal found that the donated lacquerware includes 21 first-grade, 118 second-grade and 15 third-grade artefacts. Among the gifts, the plain one-colour lacquer of the Song and Yuan, the carved ribbed (tixi) lacquer of the early Ming, the incised-gold inlaid lacquer of the Jiajing and Wanli reigns, and the mid-Qing wares represented by Qianlong's reign are all extremely precious examples of the art.

As you look at this plate, first take in the children-at-play design carved after layer upon layer of lacquer was applied, then consider how this piece of carved lacquer passed from a Yuan craftsman's hands to the present day and into the Zhejiang Museum through the Cao donation - craftsman, collector and museum, all joined by a single lacquer object.

tang-guqin-tradition.name: Tang-Dynasty Guqin and the Saying 'The Tang Is Round'

blocks.text: Tang-dynasty guqin are the earliest reliably dated instruments among surviving zithers, and rare treasures within China's guqin-making tradition. 'The Tang is round' (Tang yuan) is an old saying about guqin form that has come down to our own day.

Guqin making advanced enormously in the Tang. The 'Jiuxiao Huanpei' and 'Dasheng Yiyin' zithers made for the Tang imperial family by the Lei family of Sichuan are celebrated surviving instruments, and Tang zithers have been prized in every age as rare treasures. Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated are those made in the Tang, and nearly twenty Tang instruments survive today.

On the matter of guqin form, the ancients spoke of 'the Tang is round'. Roundness is indeed one feature of Tang zithers, but the saying is not exact - not every round-bodied zither is a Tang instrument. The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi', one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum, belongs to this group of surviving Tang zithers.

When you look at a Tang zither in the gallery, first take in its rounded outline, crackle patterns and name, then weigh the precision behind the old saying 'the Tang is round' - roundness is one feature of Tang instruments, but not the only criterion.

zhijiang-campus.zhejiang-wannian-guobao.name: Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang and the Five National Treasures

blocks.text: At the Zhijiang Campus, take 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' as your main thread for reading Zhejiang's whole history. As you enter, first remember 'three galleries, one road through ten thousand years'; then walk from the prehistory on the first floor up to the modern era on the second, and finally make a point of turning back to examine the five national treasures barred from overseas exhibition. That is all it takes to tie the whole visit together.

The Zhijiang Campus is the new main venue of the Zhejiang Museum, located in the Zhijiang Cultural Center and open to the public since 29 August 2023, covering about 54,400 square metres with a floor area of 100,000 square metres. The permanent exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' occupies the first and second floors, divided into three galleries - 'From Prehistory to the Sui and Tang Dynasties', 'Wuyue and the Two Song Dynasties', and 'From the Yuan, Ming and Qing Dynasties to the Modern Era' - tracing Zhejiang's history from the Paleolithic to 1921. It opened in August 2023.

All five groups of artefacts from the Zhejiang Museum on the list barred from overseas exhibition are found in this one exhibition. In other words, walk the length of 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang' and you will see all five national treasures in a single visit.

zhijiang-campus.fuchun-shanshui.name: Between Mountain and Water: The Digital Exhibition of the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains

blocks.text: In this tour of the Zhijiang Campus, bring your gaze back to a single painting: the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll' of the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains. When you view it, first look at the short opening section left by the fire, then at the texts and digital reconstructions beside it, and imagine what the originally complete long scroll of the Fuchun River must have looked like.

The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains is the work of Huang Gongwang, a painter active at the end of the Song and beginning of the Yuan, painted between 1347 and 1350 against the backdrop of the Fuchun River in Zhejiang. It is his masterpiece, praised by later generations as the 'Lanting of painting' and the 'supreme divine work of landscape painting', and one of China's ten greatest surviving paintings. The small opening section, repaired, is known as the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll', 51.4 cm wide and 31.8 cm high, about one-fourteenth of the original; the longer section is the 'Scroll for Master Wuyong', 636.9 cm wide and 33 cm high, about twelve-fourteenths of the original.

The Remaining Mountain Scroll and the Scroll for Master Wuyong were shown at the Taipei palace museum on 2 June 2011, but the two reunited originals were not joined together; instead they were displayed side by side in a single case sixteen metres long. The Zhejiang Museum treasures precisely the Remaining Mountain Scroll, and it, too, was chosen among the museum's top ten treasures.

zhijiang-campus.taigu-guqin.name: Sound of Antiquity: The Guqin Gallery

blocks.text: Before the guqin cases, there is no need to rush to the labels. Grow quiet first: study the crackle patterns, inscriptions and names on the instruments, then listen for the faint audio cues by the cases, and you will feel how the guqin, as a 'tradition of listening', has been preserved on a wooden body lacquered over.

The art of the guqin was inscribed by UNESCO on the second Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 7 November 2003. On 20 May 2006, the State Council added the guqin to the first national intangible cultural heritage list, classified under 'folk music', number II-34.

Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated are those of the Tang dynasty; nearly twenty Tang zithers survive today and have been treasured in every age. In the Song and Yuan periods distinct schools of guqin began to emerge; the first, the Zhe school, appeared in the late Southern Song, founded by Guo Mian. The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi', one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum, belongs to this group of surviving Tang instruments.

gushan-campus.zhongyuan-wenge.name: A Museum in a Garden, a Garden in a Museum, and the Wenglan Pavilion

blocks.text: When you come to the Gushan Campus, first treat it as a 'museum within a garden': walk west to the foot of the Wenglan Pavilion, stand where the lake and hills meet the pavilion, and see how a museum can coexist almost without a boundary with the scenery of West Lake.

The Gushan Campus is the oldest campus of the Zhejiang Museum, at the southern foot of Solitary Hill by West Lake in Hangzhou, adjoining the Bai Causeway and 'Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake' to the east and the Xiling Seal Art Society to the west. Completed in the autumn of 1993 and covering 20,400 square metres, its buildings form the layout of 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum'. It also includes the Zhejiang West Lake Art Museum and the Wenglan Pavilion.

The Wenglan Pavilion stands on the west side of the campus. Built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong reign), it was one of the seven imperial pavilions holding copies of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku Quanshu) in the Qing dynasty. Destroyed by fire in 1861 (the 11th year of the Xianfeng reign) and rebuilt in 1880 (the 6th year of the Guangxu reign), it is the only survivor of the three southern pavilions. In 2001 the State Council designated it a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; in 2006 it underwent the largest restoration since the founding of the People's Republic, and it reopened in June 2013.

gushan-campus.kunshan-pianyu.name: Jade Fragments from Mount Kun: The Ceramics Gallery

blocks.text: In the ceramics gallery of the Gushan main building, take the phrase 'jade fragments from Mount Kun' as your cue for this stretch of exhibits: from the Yue kiln's 'like jade, like ice' to the powder blue and plum green of Longquan, comparing the glazes as you go is a shortcut to understanding the celadon of Zhejiang.

The permanent exhibition 'Jade Fragments from Mount Kun - A Showcase of Ancient Chinese Ceramics' is housed in the ceramics gallery of the Gushan main building, with a display area of more than 1,200 square metres and nearly 400 ceramic artefacts on view.

The Yue kiln was a porcelain kiln of Shaoxing's Yue Prefecture in Zhejiang during the Tang and Five Dynasties, with its main sites around Shanglin Lake in Cixi. In his Classic of Tea, the Tang writer Lu Yu wrote: 'For bowls, Yue Prefecture is the finest. Its porcelain resembles jade and ice.' In the late Tang and Five Dynasties, the finest Yue celadon, green as 'a thousand peaks', was reserved exclusively as tribute and so was called 'secret colour'. The Longquan kiln, by improving its glaze recipes, created unprecedented shades such as powder blue and plum green, and is generally held to have reached its golden age in the Southern Song.

In the Leifeng Pagoda gallery at the Gushan Campus, let your eye rest first on those small, exquisite Asoka pagodas: study the 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' corners and the engraved scenes on the bodies, then reflect that they once stood at the centre of the underground palace of Leifeng Pagoda - a little pagoda is a chapter of the Buddhist kingdom of Wuyue.

Leifeng Pagoda was built under the direction of King Qian Chu of Wuyue in the Five Dynasties, enshrining a relic said to be the Buddha's spiral hair. The underground palace, directly below the pagoda's central chamber, was opened on 11 March 2001. It was a brick-built vertical shaft with an iron reliquary casket at its centre. The underground palace yielded 51 groups of artefacts; among them, the gilded pure-silver Asoka Pagoda is one of the most important objects from the site, its body holding a golden container that presumably enshrined the Buddha's spiral-hair relic.

Most of the many artefacts unearthed at Leifeng Pagoda in 2000-2001 are now collected and displayed at the Zhejiang Museum. Both Asoka pagodas are square in form, composed of a base, a body, four banana-leaf 'mountain flowers' and a spire, with scenes from the Buddha's jataka stories engraved on all four sides of the body.

huang-binhong-memorial.qixialing.name: Huang Binhong's Later Years at Qixia Ridge

blocks.text: Standing before the memorial room at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, first picture an 85-year-old man coming south in the summer of 1948: it was here that he lived out the last seven years of his life. Look at the paintings and inscriptions inside, and connect these works with those 'last seven years' to feel the mood of his late creative life.

The Huang Binhong Memorial Room stands at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, Hangzhou. In the summer of 1948, the 85-year-old Huang, invited by the National Hangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, came south from Beiping and spent the last seven years of his life here. The memorial room formally opened to visitors in 1988.

Huang Binhong (27 January 1865 - 25 March 1955) was a modern Chinese landscape painter. He died on 25 March 1955 and was buried in the Nanshan Cemetery in Hangzhou. Today a Huang Binhong memorial hall stands at the foot of Qixia Ridge, and the Huang Binhong Art Museum and Huang Binhong Park have been built in Jinhua.

huang-binhong-memorial.wuqian-zuoping.name: Five Thousand Works and the Memorial Room

blocks.text: Faced with the astonishing number of works this old painter left behind in the memorial room, first think what the sheer quantity means: he gave his life's effort to Zhejiang and became one of the great pillars of the Zhejiang Museum's collection.

After Huang Binhong's death, his family, honouring his last wish, donated all his more than five thousand works and over ten thousand artefacts, manuscripts and other belongings to the Zhejiang Museum, forming an important source of the museum's painting and calligraphy collection.

On 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated his collections to the museum: 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals. In March 1958, the Zhejiang Museum established the 'Huang Binhong Memorial Room'.

sha-menghai-residence.longlu-du.name: The Former Residence of Sha Menghai on Longyou Road

blocks.text: At the gate of Sha Menghai's former residence, first look at the five-character plaque on the stone wall inside the courtyard, then take in the brick-and-timber structure of this two-storey villa. The home of a calligrapher and seal carver tends to resemble his brush and knife - every tree and blade of grass in the courtyard seems quiet and refined.

The former residence of Sha Menghai stands at No. 15 Longyou Road, Hangzhou, covering 870 square metres with a total floor area of 601 square metres, a two-storey villa of brick-and-timber construction. The five-character plaque reading 'Former Residence of Sha Menghai' in the courtyard was written by the seal carver and calligrapher Qian Juntao. It formally opened to visitors in November 2004.

Sha Menghai (11 June 1900 - 10 October 1992) was a celebrated Chinese calligrapher and seal carver. Originally named Sha Wenruo, with the courtesy name Menghai, he came from Sha village, Tangxi township, Yin County, Zhejiang (today's Yinzhou District, Ningbo). In his later years his ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep, and his former residence lies in a quiet courtyard on Longyou Road in Hangzhou.

sha-menghai-residence.shufa-zhuanke.name: Calligraphy, Seal Carving and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Standing before Sha Menghai's former residence, widen your view to the Zhejiang Museum: the relationship between this master's calligraphy and seal carving and the museum can be read in a life packed with posts and responsibilities.

Sha Menghai's ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep: in August 1953 he became concurrently head of the museum's history department, and in August 1984 he was appointed honorary director. He also became a professor of calligraphy and seal carving at the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1963, was elected director of the Xiling Seal Art Society in 1979, and served as head of the Xiling Academy of Calligraphy and Painting in 1980.

Sha Menghai kept close company with the other great names of the Zhejiang Museum, and his works, together with those of Huang Binhong and Wu Changshuo, make up the museum's holdings of painting, calligraphy and seals. As you look at these works in the galleries, you will see how calligraphy, seal carving and the cultural institutions of Zhejiang are bound together in one bond of destiny.
